claim: Only about 15,500 of roughly 36.1 million YouTube channels - 0.043% - average above a US median wage from advertising, and 31.7 million channels (88% of the platform) earn nothing at all.
stance_target: The share of creators earning a living wage from platform advertising is a small fraction of one percent
scope_conditions: Estimated by distributing Google's disclosed USD 8.25 billion of 2019 YouTube channel payouts across subscriber tiers in proportion to the view distribution observed in a 36-million-channel crawl; the authors flag that views are a stand-in for revenue and that CPMs vary by geography and content category; advertising revenue only, excluding sponsorship, merchandise and off-platform income
quoted_support: Taking the highly uneven distribution of views as a stand-in for revenue, we see that only a small fraction of channels can expect to earn a living wage from advertising income. ... Our numbers indeed show a steep income pyramid where the lower tiers are basically working for free.
numbers: USD 15 billion total 2019 YouTube ad revenue
region: Global platform; the underlying revenue disclosure is Google-wide

claim: The 153,000 YouTube channels with at least 100,000 subscribers account for 62% of all views on a platform of over 36 million channels.
stance_target: Attention on creator platforms is concentrated in a fraction of a percent of participants
scope_conditions: Derived from a 36-million-channel crawl conducted at the end of 2019
quoted_support: Given their relatively low contribution to overall view numbers—the 153,000 channels on the top account for 62% of all views

claim: Only 2.55% of YouTube video descriptions contain a crowdfunding link, versus 49% containing a cross-platform social link, so direct fan funding is a marginal practice even among elite channels.
stance_target: Fan funding platforms like Patreon are a widespread creator revenue source
scope_conditions: 136,909,228 videos from 153,770 channels each with 100,000+ subscribers, published 2007-2020; domain-level classification, not URL-pattern level, so it may undercount; the sample is skewed toward popular channels which the authors say inflates monetization-link rates relative to a random sample
quoted_support: we found that 68% of video descriptions contain at least one link and, respectively, 44.2% for intra-platform, 49% for cross-platform, 13.4% for marketplace, and 2.55% for crowdfunding links.
numbers: 7% in Mathur et al. random sample
18% in Hua et al. English-language sample

claim: 83.1% of YouTube channels with over 100,000 subscribers never use a crowdfunding link even once, and only 1.74% use one habitually, so the standard narrative of creators diversifying into fan funding does not describe most successful creators.
stance_target: Successful creators routinely diversify into off-platform fan funding
scope_conditions: 153,770 channels with 100k+ subscribers, end-2019; measures links in video descriptions only, so funding solicited in-video, in pinned comments or via channel banners is invisible
quoted_support: For crowdfunding, the numbers are even lower: 127,805 (83.1%) channels do not use crowdfunding links even once and 144,521 (94%) use them in fewer than 20% of their videos. Only 2,675 (1.74%) add crowdfunding links in 80% of their videos or more.

claim: Off-platform monetization infrastructure is materially weaker outside the West, with Indian, Indonesian and Thai channels over-represented among channels that monetize through no external links at all, and no specialised crowdfunding service existing for India.
stance_target: Western creator monetization findings generalise to Southeast Asia
scope_conditions: Based on creator-self-selected country flags, which 43.5% of the non-linking channels left blank; country analysis limited to countries with at least 100 channels in the sample, which excludes most of Africa and smaller Latin American countries; observed end-2019, so the situation may have changed
quoted_support: the infrastructure for alternative monetization in many non-Western countries remains limited, making linking less relevant. For example, we could not find specialized crowdfunding sites for India, while we did for Russia (DonationAlerts) and Brazil (APOIA.se).
numbers: 10,460 channels (6.8%) with videos but zero links
43.5% of those have no country flag set vs 21.5% among linkers
region: Explicitly contrasts Asia / Latin America / Middle East against Western channels

claim: Monetization-link practices are concentrated in Western countries, with the Global South showing much lower use of marketplace links overall, so studies of Western creators systematically overstate global monetization diversification.
stance_target: US/Western creator monetization data describes the global creator population
scope_conditions: Creator-selected country flags on channels with 100k+ subscribers; countries with under 100 channels excluded from the analysis
quoted_support: URLs in video descriptions are most heavily present in Western countries with Japan, Russia, and Vietnam constituting notable exceptions. ... Linking practices to marketplace sites (Figure 8) show an even more accentuated pattern, with German and Austrian channels standing out as monetizing particularly heavily and the Global South showing much lower use overall.
region: Cross-country comparison; Global South vs West

claim: Reliance on crowdfunding increases as creators move DOWN the subscriber hierarchy, meaning fan funding is a substitute for advertising income among weaker creators rather than a bonus stream for successful ones.
stance_target: Fan funding compensates for, rather than compounds, platform advertising income
scope_conditions: Comparison across Silver (100k-1M), Gold (1M-10M) and Diamond (10M+) tiers within the 153,770-channel sample; marketplace linking moves in the opposite direction
quoted_support: We notice that crowdfunding, in particular, grows as we move down the hierarchy, with marketplace going into the opposite direction.
numbers: Silver n=138,284, mean 2,090.65 days active, 782.3 videos
Diamond channels posted almost six times as many videos as Silver

claim: The lower tiers of the YouTube creator population function as an unpaid standing reserve of labour whose oversupply forces even top creators to keep producing, which the authors term the aspirational curve and hope labor.
stance_target: Structural explanation for why creators persist despite earning nothing
scope_conditions: Authors' interpretation of their own income-tier estimates; draws on Kuehn & Corrigan's 'hope labor' and Hindman's cumulative-advantage framing
quoted_support: The vast majority of creators are stuck on the lower rungs of what we call the “aspirational curve,” that is, the emergent distribution of success in a market where large numbers of participants are willing to perform “hope labor,” a “future-oriented investment” (Kuehn & Corrigan, 2013, p. 10) that is likely to never pan out.

claim: Only about half of the YouTube channels above the 1,000-subscriber monetization-eligibility threshold actually participate in the YouTube Partner Program, meaning the paper's own income-tier denominator (all channels above each subscriber floor) is roughly double the true population of channels that ever attempted to monetize.
stance_target: The raw subscriber-tier channel counts Rieder et al. use as their income-share denominator represent the population that actually tried to earn money on YouTube
scope_conditions: Author-stated caveat (footnote 7), citing Lyons (2021, The Verge) reporting YouTube's own disclosure of 2 million YPP members as of August 2021, against Rieder et al.'s own 2020 census of 4,415,180 channels with 1,000+ subscribers -- consistent with a roughly 45% actual-enrollment rate; the authors offer this only as a footnote caveat, not incorporated into their headline income-tier table
quoted_support: Views do not translate directly into income as cost per view for advertisers varies greatly across countries and topics. Also, only about half of the channels above 1,000 subscribers actually participate in the YPP (Lyons, 2021).
numbers: 4,415,180 channels with 1,000+ subscribers (Rieder et al. 2020 census)
time_period: channels crawled 2019-2020; YPP membership disclosed August 2021

claim: Rieder et al. explicitly state they cannot distinguish, from their data, channels that monetize solely off-platform from those that also earn YouTube-native ad revenue, meaning none of the four telemetry sources behind the sub-2% living-wage-share estimate can measure what share of a creator's total income their platform payout represents.
stance_target: Whether any existing platform-telemetry source can estimate the ratio of platform payout to total creator income for the same individuals
scope_conditions: Author-stated methodological limitation of the YouTube video-description-link method; applies specifically to distinguishing monetization channels, not to measuring income amounts from any source
quoted_support: The same limitation applies to attempts to distinguish channels that monetize solely off-platform from those that profit from YouTube-native income streams as well... Since native ads, as we have estimated in Table 1, only generate substantial revenue for a limited number of channels, there is pressure to look for other forms of income.
